chunks: The silkscreen (legend) layer. The question: What is the layer with text called?
The silkscreen, also called the legend, is the layer of ink printed on top of a board, usually white.
It carries the human-readable labels: part names like R1 and U3, outlines, polarity marks, pin-1 dots, test point names and the board revision.
It exists so that the people who build, probe and repair the board can find and orient every part.
Think of the street names and landmarks on a map. The roads exist without them, but nobody could find their way. The silkscreen labels a crowded board the same way.
A map is useless if the labels sit under a building or cover the road.
In the same way, silkscreen text hidden under a part, or ink spilled on a solder pad, causes mistakes and soldering problems.
Left, good practice: the IC has a body outline and a pin-1 dot, the refdes sits just outside the body so it stays readable after assembly, and the resistor's outline stops short of its pads.
Right, bad practice: the text is tiny and sits inside the body (hidden once the part is placed), the pin-1 mark is missing, the outline is faint, and the label for R1 runs across a pad.
The ink on the pad would be clipped by the fab, cutting the text, and any ink left would hinder the solder.
Reference designator: the label tying a part to the schematic, such as R1 or C5. Polarity mark: a symbol showing which way a part must face, like a diode bar or a "+".
Pin 1: the dot or mark showing where a chip's first pin is. Legend / nomenclature: other names for the silkscreen layer ("PCB layers and their materials").
Soldermask: the coating the ink is printed on, never on pads ("What soldermask is and does").
Picture a board with one LED and a resistor named R1.
The silkscreen draws the resistor's outline, prints "R1" beside it (not under it), and puts a mark next to the LED's cathode side.
An assembler can now place and orient both parts without the schematic. A common rule of thumb is text at least 1 mm tall with strokes at least 0.
15 mm wide, which is 15% of the height, and ink kept about 0. 15 to 0. 2 mm away from pads. That is the whole idea.
"It's the silkscreen, also called the legend or nomenclature: a layer of ink, usually white epoxy, printed on top of the soldermask.
It carries reference designators, component outlines, polarity and pin-1 marks, test points, connector labels, and the board name and revision.
Keep it off the pads, because ink on a pad blocks soldering and the fab will clip it, use legible sizes, and choose a colour that contrasts with the mask.
It's what lets people assemble and debug the board."
